name: Group attribution error
statement: Told that a group carried a measure, people infer that its members hold matching attitudes, even when the voting rule alone decided the outcome.
meaning: The claim is about a group decision and the members behind it. A proposal passes or fails, and observers read the result as the attitude of the people in the group. The paradigm used most often manipulates the rule the vote was counted under, so that the same number of supporters produces a pass in one condition and a failure in the other. Any inference that moves with the outcome under those conditions is tracking the rule rather than the members. Allison and Messick set the bias out more widely than that, across a community law, a recall election and a jury verdict. McHoskey and Miller name it the group correspondence bias, and define it as correspondent attribution from a contextually constrained group decision. The unit of the claim is the individual member, whose attitude was never shown, and the evidence is the group's result.

origin.who: Scott T. Allison and David M. Messick
origin.note: Their paper is titled "The group attribution error" and runs to pages 563 to 579 of volume 21. Elsevier sells the text, but the publisher's own article page from 2012 survives in the Wayback Machine, and its abstract was read there on 21 September 2026. The abstract reports five experiments. Members of a community that did or did not pass a water conservation law were credited with matching attitudes, however the decision was reached. Two experiments found a closer reading of attitude from decision for out-groups than for an in-group. A fourth used a recall election and a fifth a jury, whose verdict followed the vote and the rule binding it. No figure from the paper is quoted here, because only the abstract was obtained.

evidence: Six sources describe the paradigm and one of them was read in full. Mackie and Allison ran three experiments in which a group voted twice, about six months apart, with roughly the same proportion in favour each time. Their abstract reports that a rule that changed between the votes made observers think the group's attitudes had changed. MacKie, Allison, Worth and Asuncion asked people to judge the conservatism of a political group from whether it passed a liberal measure, with the rule set so that the same support passed the measure or sank it. A measure passing made the group look more liberal, and that held where the shift ran against the stereotype of the group. Allison and Kerr took the design out of the voting booth. Their participants joined a group that had or had not provided a public good, with the number of contributors held constant and the quota varied, and they judged successful groups more cooperative and competent. McHoskey and Miller tested what the bias depends on rather than whether it occurs, reporting that identification of the constraint mediated it and that processing mode moderated that identification. Corneille, Yzerbyt, Rogier and Buidin ran the vote paradigm on Belgian students judging the local section of the Front National, told the party held either 4% or 40% of the town.

replication.headline: The effect turned up again in two laboratories with no author in common with the original, and in the one paper read in full it was carried by the threatening condition.
replication.detail: Corneille, Yzerbyt, Rogier and Buidin is the only source here read in full. All their participants were told that 57% of the group had backed the proposal, and that either 50% or 67% was needed to carry it. In the first study 81 students took part and the tables analyse 64, sixteen to a cell, on a nine-point attitude scale. The outcome of the vote moved the judgment, 6.70 after a pass against 5.63 after a failure, F(1, 63) = 9.71, p < .005. Threat then qualified that. Under low threat the outcome changed nothing, 6.12 against 5.93 with t(30) below 1, while under high threat it ran 7.18 against 5.34, t(30) = 4.22, p < .001. The second study drew 83 students, changed the question and reports the interaction alone, with no main effect of the outcome. So the abstract's flat sentence about the outcome influencing inferences describes the first study and not the second. The paper removes 7 and 9 participants for failed recall checks, which does not account for the gap between those who took part and the 64 in each table. McHoskey and Miller are the second independent laboratory, and their abstract reports the bias as something to be mediated rather than as something to be shown. The same-laboratory repetitions are Mackie and Allison in 1987 and MacKie, Allison, Worth and Asuncion in 1992. No source located here prints an effect size, so nothing can be set against the 1985 result, whose own figures were not obtained.

study.cite: Corneille, O., Yzerbyt, V. Y., Rogier, A., & Buidin, G. (2001). Threat and the group attribution error: When threat elicits judgments of extremity and homogeneity. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 27(4), 437-446.

limits: No effect size for this bias appears on this page, because no source carrying one was found. Elsevier, SAGE and Guilford all sell these articles, so six of the eight sources were read as abstracts rather than as papers. Two of those abstracts came off archived publisher pages in the Wayback Machine and one off the Kent Academic Repository. Mackie, Worth and Allison's 1990 paper in Social Cognition is the one source for which no abstract was obtained. Guilford answered with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026, the archived copy of that page is a rate-limit error, and Crossref, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall hold no abstract for it. Crossref was searched by title and by bibliographic query on that date, and Europe PMC by phrase, and no meta-analysis or multi-site replication of this bias was located. Sample sizes and a participant population were obtained only for the 2001 studies, whose students were at Louvain-la-Neuve, so the reach of the finding is not something this page can speak to. Apart from Allison and Kerr, every design described here is a written scenario about a vote that did not happen. The 4% against 40% threat manipulation is a feature of a design rather than a result.
misreadings: This is not the ultimate attribution error under another name, which has its own entry at 204. Pettigrew's proposal turns on the valence of the act and on the observer being prejudiced. His abstract predicts a dispositional reading of a negative outgroup act, and for a positive one an appeal to the exceptional case, to luck or special advantage, to motivation and effort, or to the situation. Only the last of those four is situational, so reading his second prediction as a situational attribution flattens it. The group attribution error has no prejudice condition and no valence asymmetry in its statement. What it manipulates is the counting rule, and a rule change moves the inference in whichever direction it moves the result. Nor is it the fundamental attribution error with a group in place of a person, which is entry 11. McHoskey and Miller place it in the correspondence bias family and mark the difference in the same phrase, calling it correspondent attribution from a contextually constrained group decision. The constraint sits in the counting rule rather than in anyone's behaviour, and the attitudes inferred belong to members who were never observed acting at all. Their finding that identifying the constraint mediates the bias is the point of contact between the two, and their abstract also reports that observers generalised from the decision to individual members. Entry 221 maps the attribution family and leaves this member outside the map. Every study located here runs the inference in one direction, from a group's decision to its members' attitudes.

sources.text: Allison, S. T., & Messick, D. M. (1985). The group attribution error. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 21(6), 563-579. Its abstract, naming five experiments, was read on 21 September 2026 from the publisher's 2012 article page as preserved in the Wayback Machine. Elsevier sells the full text, Unpaywall records no open copy, Crossref carries no abstract, and Semantic Scholar reports that the publisher withheld one.

Mackie, D. M., & Allison, S. T. (1987). Group attribution errors and the illusion of group attitude change. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 23(6), 460-480. Its abstract was read on 21 September 2026 from the publisher's 2015 article page as preserved in the Wayback Machine. The full text is sold by Elsevier and no open copy was found.

MacKie, D. M., Allison, S. T., Worth, L. T., & Asuncion, A. G. (1992). The impact of outcome biases on counterstereotypic inferences about groups. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 18(1), 44-51. Described from its abstract at Crossref, read on 21 September 2026. SAGE answered the article with a Cloudflare challenge that day.

McHoskey, J. W., & Miller, A. G. (1994). Effects of constraint identification, processing mode, expectancies, and intragroup variability on attributions toward group members. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 20(3), 266-276. Described from its abstract at Crossref, read on 21 September 2026, which is also the source of the term group correspondence bias used here. SAGE answered the article with a Cloudflare challenge that day.

Corneille, O., Yzerbyt, V. Y., Rogier, A., & Buidin, G. (2001). Threat and the group attribution error: When threat elicits judgments of extremity and homogeneity. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 27(4), 437-446. Read in full on 21 September 2026 as the published article, posted by the second author at UCLouvain, after SAGE answered the article with a Cloudflare challenge. Every figure quoted here was read off that file.

Mackie, D. M., Worth, L. T., & Allison, S. T. (1990). Outcome-biased inferences and the perception of change in groups. Social Cognition, 8(4), 325-342. Bibliographic record only. Guilford answered the article with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026, the archived copy of that page is a rate-limit error, and Crossref, Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall hold no abstract. No claim on this page comes from it.

Allison, S. T., & Kerr, N. L. (1994). Group correspondence biases and the provision of public goods. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 66(4), 688-698. Described from its abstract in the Kent Academic Repository, read on 21 September 2026, the repository holding no file. The American Psychological Association answered both the record and the full text with an Imperva block that day.

Pettigrew, T. F. (1979). The ultimate attribution error: Extending Allport's cognitive analysis of prejudice. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 5(4), 461-476. Its abstract at Crossref, read on 21 September 2026, is the source for the contrast drawn above, including its four readings of a positive outgroup act.
